name: Taurine
lead: Taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) is a naturally occurring sulfur-containing compound found in high concentrations in muscle, heart, retina and brain. Chemically it is an amino sulfonic acid rather than a carboxylic amino acid, and because it is not incorporated into proteins it is classed as non-proteinogenic, though it is usually still called an amino acid [1]. It is made in the human liver from cysteine and methionine, and is also obtained from meat and fish [1].

Taurine is a common ingredient in energy drinks, at roughly 1 to 3 grams per serving according to Wikipedia, and is sold as a standalone supplement [1]. In fitness, recovery and longevity communities it is promoted for exercise performance, cramps, calming after training, sleep and cell protection; it is also taken by some people using anabolic steroids or other drugs as part of large supplement stacks [11][12][13][14][15].

Published reviews report small effects on some metabolic, cardiovascular and exercise outcomes, with limited and inconsistent evidence overall [2][3][5]. Wikipedia states that high-quality clinical studies on possible effects of supplementation are absent and that preliminary human studies have been inadequate because of low numbers, inconsistent designs and varied doses [1]. No study found in the sources reviewed tests taurine for facial appearance, skin or physique outcomes in healthy people.

paras: Taurine exists as a zwitterion, with a sulfonic acid group that is fully ionised at gut pH [1]. In humans it can come from biosynthesis (via cysteine sulfinic acid or the transsulfuration pathway), active uptake by a taurine transporter, and release from cells through a volume-sensitive leak pathway [1]. It is a major constituent of bile, where it conjugates bile acids, and is among the most abundant free amino compounds in excitable tissues [1][6].

Taurine is not regarded as an essential nutrient for adult humans and has no recommended intake level [1]. Cats lack the enzyme to make it and develop retinal degeneration, heart disease and other problems on taurine-free diets, which is why it is added to cat food [1].

Athletes and lifters take taurine alone or in pre-workout mixtures with caffeine, citrulline and beta-alanine [11][12][13]. A 2021 review of taurine in sports found that, among 19 studies, key results included improvements in VO2max, time to exhaustion, some time trials and anaerobic performance, while describing its effectiveness as an ergogenic aid as controversial [3]. A 2022 single-blind crossover study tested a multi-ingredient pre-workout supplement and caffeine on bench press performance, but it did not isolate taurine [16].

Energy drinks combine taurine with caffeine and other ingredients, so research on them does not isolate taurine's effects. A 2001 trial of an energy drink examined human performance and mood [17], and a 2019 randomised crossover trial in 38 adults examined acute cardiovascular and metabolic effects of an energy drink and of mixtures of its ingredients [7].

A 2023 randomised, assessor-blinded study in people with hair loss tested a supplement containing hydrolysed fish collagen, taurine, cysteine, methionine, iron and selenium, with the authors noting that amino acids including taurine might be useful in androgenetic alopecia and telogen effluvium [8]. Because the product was multi-ingredient, the effect of taurine alone is not separable.

Taurine contributes to osmoregulation and cell-volume control, bile-salt conjugation, calcium handling and antioxidant defence, and may modulate GABA-A and glycine receptors; the sources reviewed describe these as proposed actions [1][5][2]. A 2016 review notes that little is known about its neuroendocrine effects, despite widespread consumption in energy drinks [9]. A 2006 review places taurine among the four common sulfur-containing amino acids, alongside methionine, cysteine and homocysteine [6].

Cardiovascular: A 2024 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined taurine's effects on heart rate, blood pressure, ejection fraction and heart-failure functional class, stating that earlier studies had yielded inconsistent results [18]. A 2023 review states that human and animal evidence suggests possible beneficial effects on blood pressure regulation and vascular health and describes taurine as an intriguing candidate for anti-ageing strategies [5].

Metabolic and cognitive: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis examined long-term taurine supplementation and lipid and glycaemic profiles in adults with overweight or obesity [19], and a 2025 meta-analysis examined cognitive function [20]. Wikipedia notes that one review of preliminary human studies found taurine had preventive effects on biomarkers of metabolic syndrome [1].

Ageing: A 2023 paper in Science, 'Taurine deficiency as a driver of aging', reported on the relationship between declining taurine levels and ageing, which is the origin of much recent longevity interest [21]. The relevance of this animal-and-observational work to supplementation in healthy adults has not been established by trials in the sources reviewed.
Appearance: No trial tests taurine for skin, facial structure or body composition in healthy adults.

Human trials exist but are mostly small and heterogeneous. They include exercise studies in a 2021 review of 19 studies [3], blood-pressure and cardiac function trials meta-analysed in 2024 [18], and trials of energy drinks and caffeine-taurine combinations [7][16][17][22]. Registered trials include a completed study of taurine as a possible anti-ageing therapy on oxidative stress in 24 people (NCT05149716) [23], a completed trial of low-dose caffeine and taurine effects on performance (NCT07466654, n=32) [24], and a phase 2 trial in type 2 diabetes (NCT04874012, n=94, recruiting) [25]. Wikipedia concludes that high-quality clinical studies on supplementation are absent from the literature [1].

Wikipedia reports that the European Food Safety Authority said it may be safe to consume up to 6 grams of taurine per day, that other sources consider up to 3 grams per day safe for healthy adults, and that a 2008 review found no documented health effects, positive or negative, from the taurine amounts in energy drinks [1]. EFSA also classifies pure taurine as a skin and eye irritant and skin sensitiser [1].

Concerns about energy drinks mostly relate to caffeine and the combination of ingredients. A 2021 review notes that regular consumption of energy drinks raises blood pressure and can cause tachycardia and nervousness [4], and the 2019 crossover trial examined acute cardiovascular and metabolic changes in young adults after an energy drink [7]. A 2023 trial of Red Bull examined cardiovascular and cerebrovascular responses in young adults [22].

Taurine was first isolated from ox bile in 1827 by Friedrich Tiedemann and Leopold Gmelin, who initially treated it by analogy with asparagine; Demarcay used the name taurine in 1838, and Edmund Ronalds identified it in human bile in 1846 [1][2]. Its addition to infant formula from the early 1980s, Wikipedia notes, has never been rigorously studied [1]. In the 21st century its use spread through energy drinks, and in the 2020s interest in taurine and ageing grew after the 2023 Science paper [21].

On T Nation, taurine appears in pre-workout mixtures, as a suggested calming supplement after hard training (a poster cites a coach recommending it), and for cramps, where one user mentions pickle juice and taurine [11][12][13][14]. Users on steroid or hormone regimens list large daily taurine amounts alongside magnesium, glycine and other compounds [15][26][27]; one poster says they were advised on another forum to take 2 g three times a day with magnesium [28]. These posts are anecdotal. Posters also note taurine in the context of sleep difficulties during TRT recovery [10].

lore.intro: On T Nation, taurine is mainly a background supplement in pre-workout stacks, in sleep or calming routines and, for steroid users, in long daily lists. [11][12][13][15]

claims.believers: Lifters include it in pre-workout mixtures with citrulline, beta-alanine and caffeine [11][13][14].
claims.experts: A 2021 review of 19 studies reported improvements in some endurance and anaerobic outcomes while calling its ergogenic effect controversial [3].

claims.claim: Taurine calms the nervous system and helps sleep after hard training.
claims.believers: A poster says a strength coach suggested taking taurine after an intense workout to help the brain calm down [29].
claims.experts: Reviews describe taurine as possibly modulating GABA and glycine receptors, but a 2016 review says little is known of its neuroendocrine effects [1][9].

claims.believers: One user takes pickle juice and taurine for calf cramps [12].
claims.experts: No trial on cramps was identified in the sources reviewed.

claims.claim: Large daily doses protect the heart and body during steroid use.
claims.believers: Posters on anabolic regimens list several grams of taurine a day and say they follow advice from other forums [15][26][28].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses show inconsistent cardiovascular findings in the general population [18], and no study tests taurine in people using anabolic steroids.

claims.believers: Interest in longevity circles follows the 2023 Science paper.
claims.experts: The 2023 paper argued that taurine deficiency drives ageing; a 2023 review calls taurine an intriguing anti-ageing candidate but evidence in healthy adults comes mostly from animal and small human studies [5][21].
